An exact equation for the bound

At every moment, the best bound sits where the expected cost at the moment of decision, weighted by cosh² y over the evidence below the bound, integrates to one quarter.

the bound at a constant cost of 0.1, where the equation is sinh 2b + 2b = 1/c
1.344
the mean decision time from the normalized speed measure at that cost (chapter 6's look-ahead)
0.546
the mean decision time from 0 at that cost, for comparison
1.17
Live platesThe frozen rule touches from belowFloor, cap, and smooth fitThe band the bound can't leaveThe area, integrated up to the boundOne equation, on your scheduleSame algebra, two diffusions

At every moment, the best bound sits where the expected cost at the moment of decision, weighted by cosh² y over the evidence below the bound, integrates to one quarter. That is Proposition 4, the paper's first contribution, and it holds for every continuous cost that stays between two positive constants. It takes three steps: an envelope identity that says what the value's curvature term is (the expected cost at the moment of decision), two regularity facts the paper proves rather than assumes (the bound is Hölder continuous, and smooth fit holds), and one integration from the center to the bound. The equation has no derivative of the bound in it, which makes it easy to linearize, as chapter 6 does.

One credit applies to every page of this chapter. The two identities behind the equation appear, for smooth terminal losses, in Campbell and Engelund (2026), and in their symmetric infinite-horizon setting with smooth terminal losses, their identities and smooth fit would give a relation like it. Their hypotheses exclude this model's 0-1 loss. The paper proves the identities, the regularity, and the equation for the 0-1 loss, and doesn't list the equation among its new results.

The cost at the moment of decision

Write V(t,y) for the value of starting a decision at time t with evidence y (chapter 3), and τt,y∗ for the optimal decision time from there: the first time the evidence reaches the best bound b(t+s). Below the bound, how fast the value changes with the start time is the cost now minus the expected cost at the moment of decision. That is Lemma 2:

Vt(t,y)=c(t)−Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)],LV(t,y)=Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)].

The second identity follows from the first and the backward equation Vt+LV=c. In words: the value's curvature term, LV=12Vyy+tanh⁡(y)Vy, is the expected cost at the moment of decision. For a constant cost, it is just c, as in chapter 3; for a cost that changes, it depends on the cost after t.

The argument is an envelope theorem. Hold the optimal rule from (t,y) fixed and slide the start time to t′. The reward that frozen rule earns, J(t′), can't beat the best rule from t′, so J(t′)≤V(t′,y), with equality at t′=t. A curve that stays below another and touches it at one point has the same slope there. When only the start time moves, the cost paid changes over the whole decision, but its derivative involves only the costs at the two ends.

The plate asks a question first. Then scrub the proof: each step redraws the plate, from the program's value on the test schedule from the paper's code (the “smooth step” of tests/test_exact_equation.py).

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 5

Below the bound, the value is smooth and solves the backward equation.

Work with the signed value U(t,x)=V(t,|x|)−∫0tc(u)du, so a rectangle can contain x=0: stopped at the exit from a closed rectangle inside the continuation set, it is a martingale, and the uniformly parabolic Dirichlet problem there has a smooth solution equal to it. So V is smooth in y, continuously differentiable in t, Vy(t,0)=0, and Vt+LV=c. (The paper extends the cost to t<0 by c(0), so t=0 is an interior time.)

Step 2 of 5

Freeze the optimal rule from one start, and use it from other start times.

Fix (t,y) below the bound and freeze its optimal stopping time τ=τt,y∗. For any start time t′, using that same τ earns J(t′)=Ey[g(Yτ)−∫0τc(t′+s)ds], so J(t′)≤V(t′,y), with equality at t′=t.

Step 3 of 5

Moving the start changes the cost paid over the whole decision, but its derivative involves only the costs at the two ends.

Differentiate: ddt′∫0τc(t′+s)ds=c(t′+τ)−c(t′), so J′(t)=c(t)−Eyc(t+τ). (The difference quotients are bounded by 2cmax, so the derivative passes inside the expectation.)

Step 4 of 5

A curve that stays below another and touches it has the same slope there.

V−J≥0 has a minimum at t, and both are differentiable there, so Vt(t,y)=J′(t)=c(t)−Ey[c(t+τ∗)].

Step 5 of 5

Subtract from the backward equation.

From Vt+LV=c: LV(t,y)=Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)]. The value's curvature term is the expected cost at the moment of decision.

Campbell and Engelund (2026) have both identities for smooth terminal losses: their Corollary 4.3 gives the curvature of the value in the continuation region, and their identity (6.14) gives Vt on an infinite horizon. Their hypotheses exclude this model's 0-1 loss, which has a kink, so the paper proves the identities directly for it.

The paper's lemma, and the paragraph after it

The envelope identity. In the continuation region, the value is smooth and satisfies the backward equation Vt+LV=c. The time derivative has a simple form.

Lemma 2 (Envelope identity).

At every point (t,y) with 0≤y<b(t), V is smooth in y and continuously differentiable in t, Vy(t,0)=0, and

(12)Vt(t,y)=c(t)−Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)],LV(t,y)=Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)].

The first identity is an envelope theorem: if the optimal stopping time from (t,y) is held fixed while the start time moves, the reward it earns is a lower bound for V that touches it at t, so the two have the same derivative there, and that derivative only involves the cost paid at the start and at the end. With Vt+LV=c, it gives the second identity. In words, the value's curvature term LV, which equals c for a constant cost, is the expected cost at the moment of decision.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 312–332

The full proof, from Appendix A

The continuation set C={(t,y):V>g}={y<b(t)} is open. Work with the signed value U(t,x)=V(t,|x|)−∫0tc(u)du on the open set {|x|<b(t)}, which contains x=0. Before the optimal stopping time, the value process is a martingale (the standing facts above), so for any closed rectangle R inside this set, U(t+s∧σ,Xs∧σ) is a martingale, where σ is the exit time of (t+s,Xs) from R. The operator ∂t+12∂x2+tanh⁡(x)∂x is uniformly parabolic with smooth coefficients, so the Dirichlet problem on R with the continuous data U on its parabolic boundary has a solution that is smooth inside R and continuous up to its boundary, and by the martingale property it equals U (as in Peskir and Shiryaev, 2006, Sec. 7.1). Hence U is smooth in the interior, even in x, and Ut+12Uxx+tanh⁡(x)Ux=0. Returning to V, it is smooth in y, continuously differentiable in t, Vy(t,0)=0, and Vt+LV=c.

Fix (t,y)∈C and τ=τt,y∗. For every t′,

(31)V(t′,y)≥J(t′):=Ey[g(Yτ)−∫0τc(t′+s)ds],

with equality at t′=t. The difference quotients of J are dominated by 2cmax, and ddt′∫0τc(t′+s)ds=c(t′+τ)−c(t′), so J′(t)=c(t)−Eyc(t+τ). Since V−J≥0 has a minimum at t and both are differentiable there, Vt(t,y)=J′(t). The second identity follows from Vt+LV=c.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1321–1342

What the lemma covers. Points strictly below the bound, for a continuous cost between two positive constants. At the bound itself it says nothing: how the value meets the reward for deciding there is smooth fit, on the next page.

How smooth the bound has to be

The equation comes from integrating the curvature identity up to the bound, and that step uses how the value meets the reward for deciding there. The paper proves what it needs rather than assuming it. Write W=V−g≥0 for the value of being allowed to wait; it is 0 at and above the bound. Proposition 3 says three things.

  • (a) Nondegeneracy: W(t,y)≥cmin(b(t)−y)2 below the bound. The value of waiting grows at least like cmin times the squared distance to the bound.
  • (b) Hölder continuity: |b(t)−b(t′)|≤(cmax−cmin)/cmin|t−t′|1/2. The bound can't jump, however fast the cost moves.
  • (c) Smooth fit: at every time, Vy(t,y)→g′(b(t)) as y↑b(t). The value meets the reward for deciding with a matching slope.

Part (b) follows from (a) and Lemma 1(d) in one line. Part (c) uses (b) through the law of the iterated logarithm and a coupling: the one-dimensional case of De Angelis and Peskir's (2020) mechanism, which derives smooth fit from the regularity of boundary points alone. The plate beside the proof uses the test schedule from the paper's code, a cost of 0.1 that rises toward 0.4 around time 1.5, so cmin=0.1, cmax=0.4, and the constant in (b) is 3.

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 5

Below the bound, the curvature term of the value of waiting is at least the lowest cost.

(a) By Lemma 2 and Lg=0, LW=LV≥cmin below the bound, so (cosh2⁡yWy)′≥2cmincosh2⁡y.

Step 2 of 5

Integrate twice from the bound: a parabola sits under the value of waiting.

Integrate from y to z<b and use Wy(z)≤0 (Lemma 1(a)): −cosh2⁡yWy(y)≥2cmin∫yzcosh2⁡udu≥2cmincosh2⁡y(z−y). Let z→b: −Wy(y)≥2cmin(b−y). Integrate once more, with W(t,b)=0: W(t,y)≥cmin(b−y)2.

Step 3 of 5

At one time's bound, the other time's value of waiting is caught between a floor and a cap.

(b) Suppose b(t′)>b(t) and look at y=b(t). There W(t,y)=0, while (a) at time t′ gives W(t′,y)≥cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2. Lemma 1(d) caps the difference at (cmax−cmin)|t′−t|. So cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2≤(cmax−cmin)|t′−t|.

Step 4 of 5

A path that starts just below the bound crosses it almost at once.

(c) By (b), the bound can rise by at most Ks in time s, with K=1+(cmax−cmin)/cmin. Start a coupled path at b−ϵ: since its drift is nonnegative, it is at least b−ϵ+Bs, and by the law of the iterated logarithm Bs exceeds 2Ks at arbitrarily small s. So the path crosses the bound almost at once: τϵ→0.

Step 5 of 5

Compare the starts at the bound and just below it under one stopping time: the slopes match.

Since τϵ is a stopping time for both starts, V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)≥E[g(Yτϵ0)−g(Yτϵϵ)], and the integrand is never negative, because Yϵ≤Y0 and g is increasing; so leaving out an event only lowers the right side. On the event that the lower path doesn't reach 0 first (no reflection), the two paths stay at least ϵ apart, and since g′ is decreasing, the integrand is at least ϵg′(Yτϵ0). As ϵ→0, that event has probability tending to 1 and Yτϵ0→b, so lim infϵ→0[V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)]/ϵ≥g′(b), and W(t,b−ϵ)/ϵ→0. Because cosh2⁡yWy is nondecreasing and Wy≤0, Wy has a limit at the bound, and the mean value theorem makes it 0: Vy→g′(b). That is smooth fit.

Now a much steeper schedule: Figure 1(a)'s 16-fold rise, where the cost changes almost at once. Guess what the bound can do before the plate shows it.

The constant in (b) isn't claimed to be sharp, and on Figure 1(a) it is far from it. What (b) rules out is a jump: the bound is continuous for every cost the assumption allows. The paper claims no more regularity than this for the exact bound.

The paper's proposition, and the paragraphs after it

Regularity. Write W=V−g≥0 for the value of being allowed to wait. On [0,b(t)), LW=LV≥cmin by (12), and W is nonincreasing by Lemma 1(a). Integrating (cosh2⁡yWy)′=2cosh2⁡yLW shows that W grows at least quadratically away from the bound. Combined with the Lipschitz bound in time, this pins down the bound's regularity.

Proposition 3 (Regularity).
  • (a)

    Nondegeneracy. W(t,y)≥cmin(b(t)−y)2 for 0≤y≤b(t).

  • (b)

    Hölder continuity. |b(t)−b(t′)|≤(cmax−cmin)/cmin|t−t′|1/2 for all t,t′≥0.

  • (c)

    Smooth fit. For every t≥0, Vy(t,y)→g′(b(t)) as y↑b(t).

Part (b) follows from (a) and Lemma 1(d) in one line: if b(t′)>b(t), the point y=b(t) has W(t,y)=0 and W(t′,y)≥cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2, while the two differ by at most (cmax−cmin)|t−t′|. Part (c) uses (b): since the bound can rise by at most a constant times s in time s, the law of the iterated logarithm makes the evidence cross it immediately from any boundary point, and a coupling argument then gives smooth fit. This is the one-dimensional case of the mechanism of De Angelis and Peskir (2020), who derive smooth fit from the probabilistic regularity of boundary points alone.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 334–357

The full proof, from Appendix A

(a) Fix t and write b=b(t) and W=V−g on [0,b). By Lemma 2 and Lg=0, LW≥cmin, so (cosh2⁡yWy)′=2cosh2⁡yLW≥2cmincosh2⁡y. For y<z<b, integrating and using Wy(z)≤0 (Lemma 1(a)),

(32)−cosh2⁡yWy(y)≥2cmin∫yzcosh2⁡udu≥2cmincosh2⁡y(z−y).

Letting z→b gives −Wy(y)≥2cmin(b−y). Integrating from y to b, with W continuous and W(t,b)=0, gives W(t,y)≥cmin(b−y)2.

(b) Let t,t′≥0 with b(t′)>b(t), and put y=b(t). Then W(t,y)=0, and by (a) at time t′, W(t′,y)≥cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2. By Lemma 1(d), W(t′,y)−W(t,y)=V(t′,y)−V(t,y)≤(cmax−cmin)|t′−t|. Exchanging the roles of t and t′ covers the other case.

(c) Fix t, write b=b(t) and K=1+(cmax−cmin)/cmin, so b(t+s)≤b+Ks by (b). For 0≤ϵ<b, let Yϵ start from b−ϵ, driven by the same B, and τϵ=τt,b−ϵ∗. Since tanh≥0 on [0,∞) and ℓ≥0, Ysϵ≥b−ϵ+Bs. By the law of the iterated logarithm, almost surely there are arbitrarily small s>0 with Bs>2Ks, and at such s, Ysϵ−b(t+s)>Ks−ϵ, which is positive once ϵ<Ks. So τϵ→0 almost surely as ϵ→0.

Since τϵ is a stopping time for both Y0 and Yϵ,

(33)V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)≥E[g(Yτϵ0)−g(Yτϵϵ)].

The integrand is nonnegative, because Yϵ≤Y0 and g is increasing. On the event Aϵ that Yϵ does not reach 0 before τϵ, there is no local time, so Y0−Yϵ=ϵ+∫(tanh⁡Y0−tanh⁡Yϵ)≥ϵ up to τϵ, and since g′ is decreasing on [0,∞) the integrand is at least ϵg′(Yτϵ0). As ϵ→0, P(Aϵ)→1 and Yτϵ0→b, so by dominated convergence lim infϵ→0[V(t,b)−V(t,b−ϵ)]/ϵ≥g′(b), that is, W(t,b−ϵ)/ϵ→0. Finally, cosh2⁡yWy is nondecreasing on [0,b) and Wy≤0, so Wy(t,y) has a limit L≤0 as y↑b. By the mean value theorem, W(t,b−ϵ)/ϵ=−Wy(t,ξϵ) for some ξϵ∈(b−ϵ,b), so L=0, which is smooth fit. This is the argument of De Angelis and Peskir (2020), specialized to a one-dimensional diffusion whose boundary points are regular by (b).

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1344–1383

One equation, checked live

Multiply the curvature identity by 2cosh2⁡y, integrate from the reflecting center to the bound, and use smooth fit, with cosh2⁡bg′(b)=12. The result is Proposition 4: for every t≥0,

∫0b(t)cosh2⁡yEy[c(t+τt,y∗)]dy=14.

The integrand is the expected cost at the moment of decision from each starting level y, weighted by cosh2⁡y. For a constant cost, the left side is c(12b+14sinh⁡2b), and the equation is the classical sinh⁡(2b)+2b=1/c of chapter 3; at c=0.1 its root is 1.344. It holds for every continuous cost between two positive constants, and it contains no derivative of the bound, which makes it easy to linearize, as chapter 6 does. The proof is four steps.

Scrub the proof

Step 1 of 4

Below the bound, the value's slope, scaled by cosh², grows at twice the weighted expected cost.

From Lemma 2 and the cosh2 identity: (cosh2⁡yVy)′=2cosh2⁡yLV=2cosh2⁡yEy[c(t+τt,y∗)] on [0,b(t)), with Vy(t,0)=0.

Step 2 of 4

Integrate from the center.

Integrate from 0 to z<b(t): cosh2⁡zVy(t,z)=2∫0zcosh2⁡yEy[c(t+τt,y∗)]dy.

Step 3 of 4

At the bound, smooth fit makes the left side one half.

Let z↑b(t). By smooth fit (Proposition 3(c)), the left side tends to cosh2⁡b(t)g′(b(t))=12, since g′(y)=1/(2cosh2⁡y).

Step 4 of 4

Divide by 2.

∫0b(t)cosh2⁡yEy[c(t+τt,y∗)]dy=14.

The equation characterizes the bound but doesn't compute it: the integrand depends on the bound's own future, through τ∗. What a page can do is check it. The plate below solves the dynamic program for your schedule, runs the policy it finds backward once more to get Ey[c(t+τ∗)] at every grid point, and integrates.

Where the left side misses 14, the miss is numerical, and it can come from three places. The grid: the program checks the evidence every Δt, so its bound sits about 0.5826Δt inside the continuous one, and the page adds back that shift, which is only its leading term. The finite horizon: the program forces a choice at time 10, and the bound falls to 0 as that time nears. The solver: the bound is interpolated between grid points, and the integral is a trapezoid sum. The paper's own test, tests/test_exact_equation.py, checks the same thing on the same grid as the plate's finer one, at six times on three schedules, and allows a miss of 1.5×10−3. Figure 1(a)'s step is 16-fold, against at most 4-fold in those three schedules, and on the same grid its residual is larger than that allowance; the plate prints it.

Where the equation stands. The two identities behind it appear, for smooth terminal losses, in Campbell and Engelund (2026), and in their symmetric infinite-horizon setting with smooth terminal losses, their identities and smooth fit would give a relation like it. Their own boundary equation is a different, Peskir-type one. Their hypotheses exclude the 0-1 loss of this model. The paper proves the identities, the regularity, and the equation for the 0-1 loss and uses the equation to prove Theorem 7; it lists the equation as its first contribution, but not among the results it calls new.

The paper's proposition, and the paragraph after it

The exact equation. Multiply the second identity in (12) by 2cosh2⁡y, integrate from the reflecting center to the bound, and use smooth fit with cosh2⁡bg′(b)=12.

Proposition 4 (Exact equation for the bound).

For every t≥0,

(13)∫0b(t)cosh2⁡yEy[c(t+τt,y∗)]dy=14.

For a constant cost, the left side is c(12b+14sinh⁡2b), and (13) is (9). In general, the equation says that the bound sits where the cosh2-weighted average, over evidence levels below it, of the expected cost at the moment of decision equals what a constant cost would require. It involves no derivative of the bound, which makes it convenient to linearize.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 359–376

The proof, from Appendix A

By Lemma 2, (cosh2⁡yVy)′=2cosh2⁡yEy[c(t+τt,y∗)] on [0,b(t)) and Vy(t,0)=0. Integrate from 0 to z<b(t) and let z↑b(t). By Proposition 3(c), the left side tends to cosh2⁡b(t)g′(b(t))=12.

The paper's credit, in its introduction…

The identities behind (4) appear, for smooth terminal losses, in recent work by Campbell and Engelund (2026), and specializing a general perturbation formula for free boundaries (Stojanovic, 1997) to this model at a constant cost formally gives the convolution form of the first-order correction; Section 8 explains both relations. Campbell and Engelund's hypotheses exclude the drift-diffusion model's 0-1 loss, so we prove the identities directly, and the explicit kernel, its transform, the theorem, the rule, and the measurements are, to our knowledge, new.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 195–201

And in its related work

The closest work is Campbell and Engelund (2026), who develop a regularity theory for two-sided stopping problems of a posterior martingale with a nonmonotone time-varying cost, on finite and infinite horizons, including an integral equation. In loss form, their Corollary 4.3 gives the curvature of the value in the continuation region, and their identity (6.14) gives ∂tV on an infinite horizon; translated to our coordinates, these are the two identities of Lemma 2. Their Proposition 8.6 uses the same smooth-fit mechanism to show that under a sinusoidal cost the bound cannot be constant, so it does not converge. Their hypotheses ask for a concave terminal loss, C2 in general and C3 for their time-inhomogeneous regularity results, whose generator image is strictly monotone on each side of a point, and a C1 cost with bounded c′/c. The 0-1 loss of the drift-diffusion model fails these: it has a kink, and its generator image vanishes away from the kink. We therefore prove the identities and the regularity directly. Their own boundary equation is a different, Peskir-type integral equation, and they do not linearize the boundary in a perturbation of the running cost; in their symmetric infinite-horizon setting with smooth losses, however, their two identities and smooth fit would also give a spatially integrated relation like (13). We prove (13) directly for the 0-1 loss and use it to prove the first-order theorem.

…

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 1156–1170

What the equation covers, and what it doesn't. Every continuous cost between two positive constants, on an infinite horizon, for this model's 0-1 loss. A deadline makes the cost infinite, and a cost that keeps rising has no upper level (The cost of time is continuous and bounded between two positive constants): the equation says nothing about either, and the plate doesn't draw them. Nor is it a formula: it can't be solved for b(t) directly.

Why cosh²

The weight cosh2⁡y is not special to this problem. For a one-dimensional diffusion with generator 12f″+μf′, scale density s′=exp⁡(−∫2μ), and speed density m=2/s′, one has (f′/s′)′=mLf. For Y, s′=sech2y and m=2cosh2⁡y. Because the reward is harmonic, g′/s′ is a constant, 12, and the same steps give

∫0b(t)m(y)Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)]dy=g′s′,

which is the exact equation times 2. So the exact equation is one case of an identity for one-dimensional problems with a harmonic reward. Remark 5 states this as “the same steps give”; turning the identity into an equation for the bound also needs reflection at the center, the envelope identity, and smooth fit, and the paper proves those only for this model.

Normalized on [0,b0], the speed density is the start law π0(y)=4c0cosh2⁡y of chapter 6, so the kernel is the decision time started from the normalized speed measure. At c0=0.1, that decision takes 0.546 time units on average, against 1.17 from 0.

Chapter 11 reuses the remark for unknown evidence reliability, where the belief u has drift u/2 in information time: s′=e−u2/2, m=2eu2/2, and Φ′/s′=1/2π. There the paper carries the equation over formally, not as a theorem: the cost in information time grows without bound, outside the assumption, and the paper proves no analog of Proposition 3 or Theorem 7 for that process.

The paper's remark
Remark 5 (Scale and speed).

The weight cosh2⁡y is half the speed density of Y. For a diffusion with generator 12f″+μf′, scale density s′=exp⁡(−∫2μ), and speed density m=2/s′, one has (f′/s′)′=mLf; here s′=sech2y and m=2cosh2⁡y. Because the reward is harmonic, g′/s′ is constant, equal to 12, and the same steps give ∫0b(t)m(y)Ey[c(t+τt,y∗)]dy=g′/s′. So (13) is an instance of a general identity for one-dimensional problems with a harmonic reward, and Lemma 6(b) says the kernel is the decision time started from the normalized speed measure on [0,b0]. Section 7 uses this for unknown reliability.

The paper's source, version 1.2, main.tex lines 378–388

Where this chapter sits

The paper's claims and the places one uses another, with this chapter's four printed heavier. The chapter uses chapter 2's reflected process Y and its strong solutions, chapter 3's standing assumption on the cost, and chapter 4's structure lemma (Lemma 1), optimal stopping facts, and optimal decision time τ∗. In turn, Proposition 4 is the equation Theorem 7 subtracts in chapter 6, and chapter 12's account of what is new says where it stands. Proposition 3 also feeds the second-order loss of chapter 7 (Proposition 10) and, with Lemma 2, the unequal-rewards extension of chapter 11; Remark 5 feeds the unknown-reliability extension there.

Exercises

Worked answers are folded under each question. Nothing is gated.

  1. Check both identities of Lemma 2 for a constant cost.

    Worked answer

    With c(t)≡c, Ey[c(t+τ∗)]=c. The first identity gives Vt=c−c=0: the value doesn't depend on the start time, as it shouldn't. The second gives LV=c, the equation solved in (9).

  2. Suppose the cost never decreases after t and rises at some point. Is Vt positive or negative below the bound?

    Worked answer

    Then c(t+τ∗)≥c(t) on every path, so Ey[c(t+τ∗)]≥c(t) and Vt≤0. It is strictly negative: if the cost is above c(t) from some time t+s0 on, then from any start below the bound, the evidence stays below the bound past s0 with positive probability, so c(t+τ∗)>c(t) with positive probability and Ey[c(t+τ∗)]>c(t). Starting later is worse. If the cost never increases after t, Vt≥0. A cost that rises briefly and then falls below c(t) can give either sign: the identity weighs the whole distribution of the cost at the moment of decision.

  3. Why can the proof freeze the stopping time while moving t′, when the optimal stopping time from t′ is different?

    Worked answer

    Because it only needs a lower bound that touches V at t. Any fixed stopping time used from any start time gives a reward at most V(t′,y), and the frozen τt,y∗ gives exactly V(t,y) at t′=t. A differentiable function that stays above another and touches it at an interior point has the same derivative there. This is the same move as the envelope theorem in economics.

  4. Derive Proposition 3(b) from (a) and Lemma 1(d).

    Worked answer

    Take b(t′)>b(t) and y=b(t). At time t, y is on the bound, so W(t,y)=0. At time t′, y is below the bound b(t′), so (a) gives W(t′,y)≥cmin(b(t′)−b(t))2. Since g doesn't depend on time, W(t′,y)−W(t,y)=V(t′,y)−V(t,y)≤(cmax−cmin)|t′−t|. Combine: (b(t′)−b(t))2≤cmax−cmincmin|t′−t|. Swapping t and t′ covers b(t′)<b(t).

  5. What does (b) say for a constant cost? And for a continuous cost that rises from c to 3c in a steep logistic step?

    Worked answer

    For a constant cost, cmax=cmin, the constant is 0, and the bound is constant, as it should be. For the step, cmin=c and cmax=3c, so the constant is 2 however steep the step is: the bound can move by at most 2|t−t′| between two times. The cost can change almost at once; the bound cannot.

  6. Why does the exact equation need smooth fit?

    Worked answer

    Integrating (cosh2⁡yVy)′ from 0 to the bound leaves the boundary term cosh2⁡bVy(b−). Smooth fit says Vy(b−)=g′(b)=1/(2cosh2⁡b), so the term is exactly 12. Without it, the right side of the equation would be unknown.

  7. Check that the equation reduces to sinh⁡(2b)+2b=1/c for a constant cost.

    Worked answer

    With Ey[c]=c: c∫0bcosh2⁡ydy=c(12b+14sinh⁡2b)=14. Multiply by 4/c: 2b+sinh⁡2b=1/c.

  8. Suppose the cost never decreases after time t. Use the equation to show that b(t)≤B(c(t)).

    Worked answer

    If c is nondecreasing from t on, then c(t+τ∗)≥c(t) on every path, so Ey[c(t+τ∗)]≥c(t) for every y. Then c(t)∫0b(t)cosh2⁡ydy≤∫0b(t)cosh2⁡yEy[c(t+τ∗)]dy=14=c(t)∫0B(c(t))cosh2⁡ydy, and since ∫0bcosh2 increases with b, b(t)≤B(c(t)). So when the cost never decreases after t, the optimal bound sits at or below the per-moment bound; when it never increases, at or above. (An exercise from the equation; the paper doesn't state it.)

  9. Can you solve the equation for b(t) directly?

    Worked answer

    No. The integrand depends on the future of the bound itself, through τ∗, the first time the evidence reaches b(t+s). The equation characterizes the bound; it doesn't compute it. Its use is that it has no derivative of b in it, so subtracting its constant-cost version gives an equation for bε−b0 that can be expanded in ε.

  10. Compute s′, m, and g′/s′ for Y, and check that the general identity gives the exact equation.

    Worked answer

    The drift is tanh⁡y, so s′=exp⁡(−∫0y2tanh⁡udu)=exp⁡(−2log⁡cosh⁡y)=sech2y, and m=2/s′=2cosh2⁡y. Then g′/s′=12sech2y/sech2y=12. The identity reads ∫0b2cosh2⁡yEy[c]dy=12, which is the exact equation times 2.

  11. For the unknown-reliability belief u, with generator 12∂u2+12u∂u and reward Φ(|u|), what replaces cosh2 and 14?

    Worked answer

    The drift is 12u, so s′=e−u2/2 and m=2eu2/2; Φ′(u)/s′=(e−u2/2/2π)/e−u2/2=1/2π. The equation would become ∫0U2eu2/2Eu[κ(θ+τ∗)]du=1/2π, as the paper writes it in Section 7. There, it is carried over formally, not proved (Unknown evidence reliability, through information time).

Common misreadings.

  • “LV equals the current cost c(t).”It does when the cost is constant from t on, and at any moment where the expected cost at the moment of decision happens to equal c(t). In general, it is the expected cost at the moment of decision, which depends on the cost after t.
  • “These identities are new.”Campbell and Engelund (2026) have both, for smooth terminal losses (their Corollary 4.3 and identity (6.14)). Their hypotheses exclude the 0-1 loss, so the paper proves them directly for it (What is new, to the paper's knowledge).
  • “Smooth fit is assumed, as usual.”The paper proves it at every time, from the Hölder bound, rather than assuming it.
  • “The bound moves like t.”(b) is an upper bound on how fast it can move, with a constant that isn't claimed to be sharp. The paper claims no more regularity than this for the exact bound.
  • “The exact equation is claimed as new.”The paper lists it as a contribution and proves it for the 0-1 loss, but its novelty sentence does not claim it: Campbell and Engelund's identities, with smooth fit, would also give a spatially integrated relation like it in their smooth-loss setting. Their own boundary equation is a different, Peskir-type one (What is new, to the paper's knowledge).
  • “It holds for deadlines.”It needs a continuous cost bounded between two positive constants. A deadline makes the cost infinite (The cost of time is continuous and bounded between two positive constants).
  • “The remark proves the exact equation for every one-dimensional diffusion.”It says the same steps give the general identity; the paper proves the equation only for this model. The claim map notes that the general case is not proved beyond “the same steps.”
